transcription.tex: A linear transformation maps vectors by matrix multiplication:\[\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}\longmapsto\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}ax+by\\cx+dy\end{pmatrix}\]
Linearity means \(T(\mathbf u+\mathbf v)=T\mathbf u+T\mathbf v\) and \(T(k\mathbf u)=kT\mathbf u\).
For example, \(M=\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\). Find the image of \((1,2)\).
\[\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}8\\3\end{pmatrix}\]
The origin stays fixed because \(M\mathbf0=\mathbf0\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: Which statements are true?\par 1. A non-zero translation in the plane can be represented by a \(2\times2\) matrix.\par 2. A linear map can change the dimension of the space.\par 3. Every linear transformation fixes the origin.

1. False: a translation moves the origin.\par 2. True: for example, \[\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}\]3. True: \(M\mathbf0=\mathbf0\).

transcription.tex: a. Find the matrix of \((x,y)\mapsto(x+2y,3x)\).
\[\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&0\end{pmatrix}\]
b. Find the matrix of \((x,y)\mapsto(-2y,3x+y)\).
\[\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\3&1\end{pmatrix}\]
Transform the square \(A(1,1),B(3,1),C(3,3),D(1,3)\) using \(M=\begin{pmatrix}-1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\).
\(A^{\prime}(1,3),B^{\prime}(-1,7),C^{\prime}(3,9),D^{\prime}(5,5)\).\par This reverses orientation and enlarges lengths by \(\sqrt5\).

transcription.tex: 1. Which maps are linear?\par a. \((x,y)\mapsto(2x,y+1)\)\par b. \((x,y)\mapsto(x^2,y)\)\par c. \((x,y)\mapsto(2x+y,x+xy)\)\par d. \((x,y)\mapsto(y,-x)\)\par e. \((x,y)\mapsto(y+3,x+3)\)\par f. \((x,y)\mapsto(2x,3y-2x)\)

a. No: constant term.\par b. No: squared term.\par c. No: product \(xy\).\par d. Yes: matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}\).\par e. No: constant terms.\par f. Yes: matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\-2&3\end{pmatrix}\).

slides.title: Determining a matrix for a transformation

transcription.tex: The columns of a transformation matrix are the images of the basis vectors.\[\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}a\\c\end{pmatrix},\quad\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}b\\d\end{pmatrix}\]
Therefore the matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\).
Find the matrix of reflection in the \(y\)-axis.
\[\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]\[\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}\]\[M=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\]

transcription.tex: A rotation through \(\theta\) anticlockwise about the origin sends the basis vectors to\[\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta\\\sin\theta\end{pmatrix}\]and\[\begin{pmatrix}-\sin\theta\\\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}\]
\[R_\theta=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}\]
\[R_{90^\circ}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{Invariant points}\par An invariant point maps to itself. Solve \(M\mathbf x=\mathbf x\).\par For reflection in \(y=x\), every point on \(y=x\) is invariant.\par For a non-identity rotation, only the origin is invariant.

\textbf{Invariant lines}\par An invariant line maps onto itself; its individual points need not stay fixed.\par Reflection in \(y=x\) preserves \(y=x\) and every line \(y=-x+c\).\par A \(180^\circ\) rotation preserves every line through the origin. Other non-identity rotations have no invariant lines.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: Find the invariant points of \(M=\begin{pmatrix}5&4\\2&3\end{pmatrix}\).
Every point on \(y=-x\) is fixed. The line is pointwise invariant.
Check by substituting \((x,-x)\) into the transformation.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

slides.title: Finding invariant lines – worked example in class

transcription.tex: Find the invariant lines of \(M=\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\5&6\end{pmatrix}\). Start with \(y=mx+c\).
For \(y^{\prime}=mx^{\prime}+c\), compare coefficients:\[5+6m=m(3+2m)\]\[6c=(2m+1)c\]\[(2m-5)(m+1)=0\]Hence \(y=\frac52x+c\) for any \(c\), or \(y=-x\). No vertical line is invariant.

transcription.tex: 6. Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\), \(B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}\).\par a. Describe both transformations.\par b. Find the image of \((3,2)\) under \(A\).\par c. If \(B(a,b)=(a-3b,2a-2b)\), find \(a,b\).
a. Reflection in the \(x\)-axis; rotation \(270^\circ\) anticlockwise about the origin.\par b. \((3,-2)\).\par c. \(b=a-3b\), \(-a=2a-2b\), so \(a=b=0\).
7. Let \(M=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}\).\par a. Describe \(M\).\par b. If \(M(p,q)=(-\sqrt2,-2\sqrt2)\), find \(p,q\).\par c. Find \(M^3\).\par d. Describe \(M^3\).

a. Rotation \(225^\circ\) anticlockwise.\par b. \(-p+q=-2,-p-q=-4\): \(p=3,q=1\).\par c. \[M^3=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}\]d. Rotation \(315^\circ\) anticlockwise. Both centres are the origin.

Reflection in \(y=x\). Since \(A^2=I\), \(A^{50}=I\).
9. A rotation has matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-1/2\end{pmatrix}\). Find the possible matrices.
\(a=-\frac12\), and the angle is \(120^\circ\) or \(240^\circ\).\[\frac12\begin{pmatrix}-1&-\sqrt3\\\sqrt3&-1\end{pmatrix}\]or\[\frac12\begin{pmatrix}-1&\sqrt3\\-\sqrt3&-1\end{pmatrix}\]

transcription.tex: 10. A rotation of \(270^\circ\) clockwise about the origin maps \((a,b)\) to \((a-5b,4b)\). Find the possible points.
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\]\[-b=a-5b,\quad a=4b\]Every point \((4b,b)\), where \(b\) is real, satisfies the conditions.
\textbf{Challenge}\par Derive the general rotation matrix using the images of \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\).
\[(1,0)\mapsto(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\]\[(0,1)\mapsto(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)\]\[R_\theta=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}\]

transcription.tex: Describe these transformations:\[A=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\]\[B=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\]
\(A\): enlargement, scale factor 3, centre the origin.\par \(B\): stretch parallel to the \(x\)-axis, factor 2.

For positive \(a,b\), \(\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\0&b\end{pmatrix}\) stretches by factor \(a\) parallel to the \(x\)-axis and factor \(b\) parallel to the \(y\)-axis.\par A negative factor also reverses that coordinate; a zero factor collapses a dimension.

Images: \((4,3),(4,6),(8,6)\).\[\text{Original area}=\tfrac12\]\[\text{Image area}=\tfrac12(4)(3)=6\]The area scale factor is \(12=\det M\).

transcription.tex: 5. Describe \(M=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&-3\end{pmatrix}\). A triangle of area \(k\) has image area 24. Find \(k\).
Stretches of factors 2 and 3 parallel to the coordinate axes, together with reflection in the \(x\)-axis.\[|\det M|=6,\quad k=24/6=4\]
8. The triangle \((a,1),(4,1),(4,3)\) is transformed by \(2\sqrt5I\). Describe the transformation and find \(a\) if its image area is 60.
Enlargement, factor \(2\sqrt5\), centre the origin.\[20|4-a|=60\]\[a=1\ \text{or}\ 7\]

transcription.tex: 9. Let \(M=\begin{pmatrix}p&1\\p&q\end{pmatrix}\), where \(q>0\), and \(M^2=6I\). Find \(p,q\).
\[M^2=\begin{pmatrix}p^2+p&p+q\\p^2+pq&p+q^2\end{pmatrix}\]\(p+q=0\), and \(p^2+p=6\), giving \(p=2\) or \(-3\). Since \(q>0\), \(p=-3,q=3\).
11. A pentagon of area 12 is transformed by \(M=\begin{pmatrix}-1&\sqrt2\\-\sqrt2&-1\end{pmatrix}\). Find the image area.
\[\det M=1+2=3\]\[\text{Image area}=36\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: 12. The triangle with vertices \((k,1),(4,1),(4,k)\), where \(k\) is an integer, is transformed by \(M=\begin{pmatrix}4&-1\\k&2\end{pmatrix}\). Its image area is 10. Find \(k\).

If \((k-4)(k-1)(k+8)=-20\),\[(k-2)(k^2+5k-26)=0\]only \(k=2\) is an integer. For the positive sign, the cubic is\[k^3+3k^2-36k+12=0\]Any integer root must divide 12; none of \(\pm1,\pm2,\pm3,\pm4,\pm6,\pm12\) works. Hence \(k=2\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: 13. Rotate the triangle \((0,0),(7,7),(3,-2)\) through \(45^\circ\) anticlockwise about the origin. Find its image, determinant and area.
\[R=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\]Images: \((0,0),(0,7\sqrt2),(5/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2)\).
\[\det R=1\]\[\text{Area}=\tfrac12|7(-2)-7(3)|=\tfrac{35}2\]The image has the same area.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Combining transformations}\par Apply \(A\) first, then \(B\):\[\mathbf x\mapsto A\mathbf x\mapsto B(A\mathbf x)\]
\[\text{Combined matrix}=BA\]
Matrix multiplication is associative: \(B(A\mathbf x)=(BA)\mathbf x\).\par It is generally not commutative: \(BA\ne AB\). The rightmost transformation acts first.

transcription.tex: 1. Reflect in \(y=x\), then stretch parallel to the \(x\)-axis by factor 4. Find the combined matrix.
\[\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&4\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\]
2. Rotate \(90^\circ\) anticlockwise, then reflect in \(y=x\). Describe the combined transformation.
\[\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\]Reflection in the \(x\)-axis.

transcription.tex: Edexcel January 2013, Q4. Let \(P\) represent rotation \(90^\circ\) anticlockwise about the origin and \(Q\) reflection in \(y=-x\). Find the matrix and transformation for \(P\) followed by \(Q\).
\[P=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}\]\[QP=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\]Reflection in the \(y\)-axis.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: 5. Show that reflection in the \(y\)-axis followed by reflection in \(y=-x\) is a rotation. Give its angle and centre.
\[\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\]Rotation \(90^\circ\) anticlockwise about the origin.

transcription.tex: 7. Let \(P=\begin{pmatrix}-4&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(Q=kI\). Find \(PQ\), describe the transformation, and compare \(PQ\) with \(QP\).

\[PQ=QP=\begin{pmatrix}-4k&0\\0&2k\end{pmatrix}\]The coordinates are multiplied by \(-4k\) and \(2k\). For \(k>0\), these are stretches of factors \(4k,2k\) with reflection in the \(y\)-axis. For \(k<0\), reflection is in the \(x\)-axis, with factors \(4|k|,2|k|\). For \(k=0\), all points map to the origin.

transcription.tex: 8. Find and describe \(A^2\), where \(A=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&4\end{pmatrix}\).
\[A^2=\begin{pmatrix}9&0\\0&16\end{pmatrix}\]Stretches by factors 9 and 16 parallel to the \(x\)- and \(y\)-axes.
Generalise for \(B=\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\0&b\end{pmatrix}\).
\[B^2=\begin{pmatrix}a^2&0\\0&b^2\end{pmatrix}\]Scale the coordinates by \(a^2,b^2\). A zero factor collapses that coordinate.

11. Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}\), \(B=5I\). A shape is transformed by \(B\) then \(A\); its image area is 75. Find the original area.
\[|\det(AB)|=25\]\[\text{Original area}=75/25=3\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: 13. Show that applying \(A=\begin{pmatrix}k&\sqrt3\\\sqrt3&-k\end{pmatrix}\) twice is an enlargement.
\[A^2=(k^2+3)I\]Enlargement, scale factor \(k^2+3\), centre the origin.
14. Generalise for \(P=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&-a\end{pmatrix}\).
\[P^2=(a^2+b^2)I\]Enlargement, scale factor \(a^2+b^2\), centre the origin. If \(a=b=0\), the plane collapses to the origin.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Transformations in three dimensions}\par The three columns are the images of \(\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k\).\par Find the matrix of reflection in the plane \(z=0\).
\[(x,y,z)\mapsto(x,y,-z)\]\[M=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&-1\end{pmatrix}\]
The \(x\)- and \(y\)-coordinates stay fixed; the \(z\)-coordinate changes sign.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Rotations in three dimensions}\par Use the right-hand convention: positive rotation is anticlockwise when looking towards the origin from the positive end of the axis.
\[R_x(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\0&\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}\]
\[R_y(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&0&\sin\theta\\0&1&0\\-\sin\theta&0&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}\]
\[R_z(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta&0\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}\]

\[BA=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-1)\]\[B=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-1)A^{-1}\]\[B=\frac1{10}\begin{pmatrix}-1&3&7\\3&1&-1\\2&-6&-4\end{pmatrix}\]
